# The Python package {#sec-python}

The package `biyos` calls the C library through `ctypes` and needs no compiled extension of its own, so one build serves every Python version from 3.10. A method takes the name of the C call it wraps, without the prefix: `BIYOS_addvar` is `model.addvar`, `BIYOS_setenvdblopt` and its kin are `env.setopt`, and the parameters keep their C names, such as `lb` and `ub`. Classes keep full names, except `Env` for the environment. Each follows the same rules as its C call, so the chapters before this one hold for Python as they do for C. This chapter covers what Python adds. [The Python API](#sec-pyapi) lists every class and method.

## Environments and models {#sec-python-handles}

`Env()` creates an environment and `Model(env)` a model on it. Both are context managers, so a `with` block frees them when it ends, and both have a `close` method that does the same. Closing an environment closes every model made on it first. Using a closed environment or model raises `ValueError`, and closing one twice does nothing.

A model keeps its environment alive, so an environment the program no longer references stays allocated while one of its models is open. An environment or a model closed from inside one of its own calls, by a hook for instance, reads as closed at once and is freed when that call returns. A model closed by a hook during any other call reads as closed at once too, and is freed when the outermost call returns, where `BIYOS_freemdl` would fail ([Inside a hook](#sec-events-inside)).

## Blocks and views {#sec-python-blocks}

`addvar`, `addfun`, `addcon`, `addobj`, `addind`, `addsos`, `addcone`, `addccon` and `addpwl` return a block: `Variables`, `Functions`, `Constraints`, `Objectives`, `Indicators`, `SpecialOrderedSets`, `Cones`, `Complements` or `PiecewiseLinears`. A block holds its model, the index of its first item and its count, so it costs the same whether it holds three items or three million. It supports `len`, iteration, indexing from either end and slicing with step 1:

```python
x = model.addvar(4)
len(x)        # 4
x[-1]         # the view of variable 3
x[1:3]        # a block of variables 1 and 2
```

Indexing a block gives a view, such as a `Variable`, which passes as its index wherever the model takes one: `int(x[2])` is 2. A whole block passes wherever the model takes a list of indices. A block or a `range` with step 1 goes to the `rg` form of the C call, two integers whatever its size, and any other sequence to the `sp` form; both give the same result, except that a range past the last item is refused even when it is empty. The model checks the family and the owner of each view and block, so passing a function where a variable is due raises `TypeError`, and a variable of another model `ValueError`, instead of naming the wrong item. `on` gives the block of the same indices in another model, such as a copy ([Copying in Python](#sec-copy-python)).

`delvar`, `delfun`, `delcon`, `delobj`, `delind`, `delsos`, `delcone` and `delccon` take a list, a range or a block, delete those items and return the map of [Deleting records](#sec-model-deleting) as a list. Once a call deletes an item, the indices of every block and view the model gave before may name other items, so the model refuses them with `ValueError`, whatever their family. A call that deletes nothing leaves them valid. `delcb` takes a list of callbacks and returns the same map; callbacks have no blocks, so it leaves every block and view valid.

## Arrays {#sec-python-arrays}

A method that takes an array accepts any sequence of the right length: a list, a tuple, a block where indices are due. A sequence of the wrong length raises `ValueError`, an entry of the wrong type `TypeError`, and an integer too large for 32 bits `OverflowError`. A writable, contiguous buffer of doubles, such as an `array.array("d")`, passes to C without a copy where doubles are due; everything else is copied into a C array for the call. The annotations name sequences, so a type checker refuses a NumPy or a ctypes array, though both work at run time: a contiguous NumPy array of float64 is such a buffer and passes without a copy, while a ctypes array of doubles is copied. `None` stands for a null array and takes the default the C call gives it.

The annotations name each number by what it stands for, as @sec-model does in C: `Real` is a `BIYOS_real`, such as a bound or a coefficient, `Index` a `BIYOS_index`, a count or an index of items, and `Offset` a `BIYOS_offset`, an offset into the terms, members or nodes of a model, or a count of them. They are aliases of `float` and `int`, so a type checker reads them as those.

The readers return lists, in the order of the C call's arrays:

| Method | Returns |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| `getvar(idx)` | kinds, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getquadterm(idx)` | functions, first and second variables, coefficients |
| `getrlinterm(idx)` | functions, variables, coefficients |
| `getclinterm(idx)` | functions, variables, coefficients |
| `getexpr(idx)` | counts, codes, arguments, values |
| `getcon(idx)` | functions, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getobj(idx)` | functions, senses, priorities, weights |
| `getind(idx)` | variables, values, functions, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getsos(idx)` | kinds, counts, variables, weights |
| `getccon(idx)` | bounded functions, complementary functions, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getpwl(idx)` | counts, abscissas, values |
| `getgpat(idx)` | counts, variables |
| `gethpat(idx)` | counts, rows |

`idx` lists the items to read, or is a block or a range of them, and defaults to every item, so `model.getvar()` reads them all. The readers of terms size their arrays themselves. `getrlinterm` reads the linear terms of functions and `getclinterm` those of variables, each term as its function, its variable and its coefficient, and `getnrlinterm` and `getnclinterm` count them. `getquadterm` reads the quadratic terms of functions in the same shape, with two variables, and `getnquadterm` counts them. `addlinterm(fun, var, coef)` adds terms in that same shape, so `target.addlinterm(*source.getrlinterm())` copies the linear terms of one model into another with the same functions and variables. `addquadterm(fun, var1, var2, coef)` does the same for quadratic terms, from `getquadterm`. `getsos` reads special ordered sets as `addsos` takes them, the members of each set after those of the one before, so `target.addsos(*source.getsos())` copies them into a model with the same variables, and `getnsosvar` counts the members. `getpwl` reads piecewise linear functions the same way, the points of each after those of the one before, so `target.addpwl(*source.getpwl())` copies them, and `getnpwlpt` counts the points. `getexpr` reads the expressions of functions in the postfix `addexpr` takes, its codes as `Operator` members, and `getnexpr` counts their entries and values, so `target.addexpr(*source.getexpr())` adds the expressions of one model to another, ready to attach ([Reading a model back](#sec-model-reading)).

`addlinterm` also takes the terms of each function as one list. When the entries of `var` are sequences, `fun` lists the functions in any order, or is a block or a range of them, and `var[j]` and `coef[j]` hold the variables and the coefficients of `fun[j]`, so no function index is repeated. The call goes to `BIYOS_addrlintermsp`, or `BIYOS_addrlintermrg` for a block or a range. `addquadterm` follows the same rule with `var1` and `var2`, and `addclinterm(var, fun, coef)` takes the functions of each variable that way only. A scalar in place of the functions, or of the variables for `addclinterm`, stands for one record, its terms one level less nested, or its one term when they are scalars too:

```python
model.addlinterm([0, 2], [[1, 2], [0]], [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0]])
model.addlinterm(0, [0, 1], [1.0, 2.0])
model.addlinterm(0, 1, 1.0)
model.addclinterm(x[2], [f[0], f[1]], [1.0, 2.0])
```

An entry of `coef` longer or shorter than its entry of `var` raises `ValueError`, as does one of `var2` against `var1`, and a scalar anywhere else `TypeError`.

A getter of an attribute takes the list of indices its setter takes and returns lists the same way: `model.getvarbnd(idx)` returns the lower and the upper bounds of the variables `idx` lists, and `model.getvarknd(idx)` their kinds. `getobjtol(idx)` returns the absolute and the relative tolerances of objectives, which `getobj` leaves out, as `addobj` does, and `getvartol(idx)`, `getcontol(idx)`, `getconetol(idx)` and `getccontol(idx)` those of variables, constraints, cones and complements, None where an item holds none. `getcst(idx)` returns the constants of functions, which `setcst` sets and `addcst` adds to.

## Expressions {#sec-python-expressions}

Arithmetic on variable views builds an `Expression`, a tree that holds its operands and computes nothing. `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `**`, unary `-` and `abs` take views, expressions and numbers, and `biyos.exp`, `biyos.log` and the other functions of `biyos` give one for each operator of [Expressions](#sec-model-expressions), down to `biyos.max` and `biyos.min`. Those two stay out of `__all__`, so `from biyos import *` leaves the builtins alone. `biyos.piecewise(p, x)` applies the pwl `p`, a `PiecewiseLinear` or its index, to `x`, and the model checks `p` when it takes the expression. An operand of any other type, a string or `None` for instance, raises `TypeError`. Dividing by a number multiplies by its inverse, so the terms stay linear, and `x[0] / 10` holds the weight `0.1`, which may differ in the last bit from the quotient written. `repr` of a variable or an expression reads as the formula, such as `x[0]**2 + 3*x[1]`, each variable written `x[i]` by its index, so it prints the same once the model is closed.

`<=`, `>=` and `==` give a `Comparison`, the constraint that the difference of the two sides lies in its bounds: `a <= b` is `a - b <= 0`, and a number on either side becomes the bound. A comparison keeps its sides in `lhs` and `rhs` and its operator in `sense`, a `ComparisonSense`, and `repr` prints it as a formula, such as `x[0]**2 <= x[1] + 1`. A number always lands in `rhs`, as a `float`, since Python hands `1 <= e` to `e` as `e >= 1`, so it reads and prints as `e >= 1`. A comparison has no truth value, so `bool(x[0] + 1 == x[1])`, an `if` on one and a chained `a <= b <= c` raise `TypeError`. The exception is `==` between two views, true when both name one variable of one model, so views serve as keys of dictionaries and sets. `==` with a value of another type, such as `None`, is False. `<` and `>` are refused, and a bound that is NaN or leaves no value, such as `x[0] <= -biyos.inf`, raises `ValueError`.

`addobj` takes an expression, a view or a list of them, and `addcon` a comparison or a list of them, its bounds from the comparisons, with `lb` and `ub` left out. Every expression of the call goes to the model in one `addexpr`, a subexpression used twice is sent once with `Operator.KEEP` and `Operator.REFERENCE`, and `attachexpr` splits off the constant, linear and quadratic terms ([Expressions](#sec-model-expressions)). A view made before a deletion, or one of another model, raises `ValueError` before anything is added.

A defined quantity can be written two ways. With `y` a variable, `y == sum(...)` is an equality constraint, a row on top of the variable `y`, which the solver keeps equal to the sum. Held in a name, `y = sum(...)` is an expression and no variable, and every expression built from `y` holds the same tree, which one `addcon` or `addobj` call sends once.

```{.python file="interfaces/python/examples/expressions.py" item="build"}
```

A pwl is data `addpwl` adds before any expression applies it, and it takes no name and is never deleted ([Expressions](#sec-model-expressions)):

## Evaluation {#sec-python-evaluation}

`evalf(x)`, `evalg(x)`, `evalh(x, w)` and `evalhv(x, w, v)` evaluate the model at the point `x` as [Evaluating a model](#sec-model-evaluating) describes, and return lists: a value for each function, one for each entry of the Jacobian pattern, one for each entry of the lower Hessian pattern, and the product, a value for each variable. `getgpat(idx)` reads the variables of the functions `idx` lists, and `gethpat(idx)` the rows of the columns `idx` lists, each record's after those of the one before, every function or column by default, and `getngpat(idx)` and `getnhpat(idx)` count those entries. The values of `evalg` follow `getgpat()`, and those of `evalh` follow `gethpat()`:

```{.python file="interfaces/python/examples/evaluation.py" item="evaluate"}
```

An `Exception` a callback raises stops the call, which raises `biyos.Error` with the code `BIYOS_ERR_CALLBACK` and the callback's exception as its `__cause__`, so the traceback shows both. Any other exception, such as `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit`, stops the call too and comes out of it unchanged, so `except Exception` does not catch it.

## Constants {#sec-python-constants}

The C constants a program passes become `IntEnum` classes with the same values and full names: `VariableKind`, `ObjectiveSense` and `SpecialOrderedSetKind` for models, `EventKind` and `EventLevel` for events, `Checking` for the values of `checking` and `OptionSource` for where a model's option comes from, so `BIYOS_EVTLVL_WARN` is `EventLevel.WARNING`. A reader returns them as members of their class, so `model.getvar()[0][0]` is `VariableKind.CONTINUOUS` rather than 1. Options are read and set by name ([Options in Python](#sec-options-python)).

## Failures {#sec-python-errors}

A failed C call raises `biyos.Error`, carrying the status as `code` and the message as its text. Mistakes the package catches before calling C raise Python's own exceptions, as [Errors in Python](#sec-errors-python) lists, and an exception raised in a hook is raised in the program once the call returns ([Events in Python](#sec-events-python)).
